title: The Aegis Fuel Supply at a Glance
lede: Aegis burns deuterium and helium-3; the helium-3 is bred on Earth by the Hyperion breeder, closing a fully domestic fuel loop.
body: The burner (Aegis) runs the deuterium–helium-3 (D–3He) reaction. Deuterium is drawn from ordinary water and is effectively unlimited. Helium-3 is the scarce partner, and Aegis does not mine it or import it: it is produced as a by-product of the breeder (Hyperion), whose bred tritium decays into helium-3 on a fixed physical clock. This pairing is the reason Aegis can be described as a sovereign power source.

The burner is at design stage. It is being perfected now, while the breeder is built (breeder construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind first tritium is expected around 2030; the first test burner follows around 2032). By the time a fielded burner needs a steady helium-3 stream, the breeder fleet is intended to be supplying it. Nothing in the burner fuel story depends on lunar mining or on a hardware net-gain claim that has not yet been demonstrated.
Helium-3: bred on Earth via tritium decay in Hyperion
Primary reaction is aneutronic; a small 5.44% neutron fraction comes from side reactions
Charged fusion products enable direct energy conversion

The pages in this section trace each link: the physics of the fuel, where each isotope comes from, how it is stored and handled, how the supply is secured, and the honest limits of what has and has not yet been built.

title: The D–3He Fuel Cycle
lede: The deuterium–helium-3 reaction releases 18.3 MeV almost entirely as charged particles, which is what makes direct energy conversion and low neutron output possible.
body: The reaction Aegis is built around is D + <sup>3</sup>He → <sup>4</sup>He (3.6 MeV) + p (14.7 MeV). Both products are charged: an alpha particle and a proton. Because charged particles are confined and steered by magnetic and electric fields, their energy can be recovered by direct energy conversion rather than only as heat. This is the physical basis for the burner's efficiency and low-signature operation.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">PRIMARY CHANNEL · ANEUTRONIC</text><rect x="60" y="60" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="135.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D + <sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="135.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">reactants</text><line x1="214" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="257.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">18.3 MeV</text><rect x="304" y="40" width="150" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="379.0" y="56.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600"><sup>4</sup>He</text><text x="379.0" y="74.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">3.6 MeV</text><rect x="304" y="104" width="150" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="379.0" y="120.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">proton</text><text x="379.0" y="138.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">14.7 MeV</text></svg>
Why it is not perfectly aneutronic

A pure D–3He plasma still contains deuterium, and deuterium reacts with itself. The D–D side reactions produce tritium and helium-3, and one D–D branch and the subsequent D–T reaction release neutrons. In the Aegis design point this shows up as a neutron fraction of 5.44% of total fusion power — low, but not zero. The fuel cycle and shielding are designed around this honest number, not around an idealized aneutronic claim.
Side: D + D → T + p and D + D → <sup>3</sup>He + n
Net neutron fraction at the design point: 5.44%

The consequence for supply is important: the burner consumes helium-3 and deuterium and returns helium-4 ash. It does not breed its own fuel. Every kilogram of helium-3 must come from outside the machine — which is exactly the role the breeder fills.

title: Why Helium-3 Is the Burner's Fuel
lede: Helium-3 lets the burner run a mostly-aneutronic reaction with charged products, trading extreme fuel scarcity for low neutron damage and direct conversion.
body: Every fusion fuel is a compromise. D–T is easy to ignite but throws 80% of its energy into 14 MeV neutrons, which activate structures and demand heavy shielding and remote handling. D–<sup>3</sup>He is far harder to burn — it needs higher temperatures and better confinement — but its primary channel is aneutronic and its products are charged. Aegis accepts the harder physics to gain a cleaner, lower-signature machine suited to fixed installations.
Low neutron output → less activation, lighter shielding, longer component life
Charged products → direct energy conversion is possible
No tritium as a primary fuel in the burner → a smaller radiological inventory on site
Cost: helium-3 is scarce and must be bred

Why the tandem mirror suits it

D–<sup>3</sup>He rewards a device that can hold a very hot, well-confined central plasma and recover charged-particle energy at the ends. The tandem mirror does both: high-field end plugs (26.49 T) build an electrostatic barrier that holds ions in the central cell, and the expanding field at the ends spreads the escaping charged flux for direct conversion. The fuel choice and the machine geometry are chosen together.

The catch is supply. p–<sup>11</sup>B is even cleaner but presently unreachable; D–<sup>3</sup>He is reachable but needs a helium-3 source. Solving that source problem on Earth is the entire point of the breeder–burner pairing.

title: Helium-3 from the Hyperion Breeder
lede: Hyperion breeds tritium; that tritium decays into helium-3 at a fixed rate, making the breeder a helium-3 generator on a 12.3-year clock.
body: The breeder is a helium-3 factory

Hyperion is a D–T spherical tokamak whose main product line is tritium — a design-point yield in the ~4 kg/yr class, with the tritium breeding ratio treated as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8. Tritium is radioactive and decays into helium-3. So a store of bred tritium is, over time, a store of helium-3 in the making. Hyperion's design-point helium-3 output is in the ~1.97 kg/yr class as this decay proceeds.

This means Hyperion serves two customers at once. Some bred tritium can be used directly (tritium is itself a valuable product for the breeder line), and the fraction allowed to decay yields helium-3 for the burner. The split between held tritium and decayed helium-3 is an inventory decision, not a physics constraint — it is set by how much helium-3 the burner fleet needs and when.
Breeder product: bred tritium (~4 kg/yr class) plus 14 MeV neutrons
Half-life fixes the conversion rate; no separation reaction is needed to make helium-3
The tritium/helium-3 split is set by fleet demand

No part of this requires the burner to be operating, and none of it claims hardware net gain. The breeder is built first (construction from Q2 2027, first tritium ~2030), and the helium-3 inventory begins accumulating from that point, ahead of the first test burner around 2032.

title: Tritium Decay to Helium-3
lede: Tritium beta-decays to helium-3 with a 12.32-year half-life, a fixed physical process that turns a tritium inventory into a helium-3 inventory.
body: Tritium (3H) is unstable. It undergoes beta-minus decay: 3H → 3He + e− + ν̄. A neutron in the tritium nucleus converts to a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, leaving helium-3. The decay energy is low — about 18.6 keV maximum electron energy — so the process is easy to shield and produces no penetrating gamma radiation. The half-life is 12.32 years.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 175" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">BETA-MINUS DECAY</text><circle cx="120" cy="95" r="34" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="120" y="92" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="14"><sup>3</sup>H</text><text x="120" y="108" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9">tritium</text><line x1="158" y1="95" x2="300" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="229.0" y="89.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">12.32 yr half-life</text><circle cx="360" cy="95" r="34" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="360" y="92" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="14"><sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="360" y="108" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9">helium-3</text><text x="470" y="80" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">+ e− (≤18.6 keV)</text><text x="470" y="105" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">+ antineutrino</text></svg>

A 12.32-year half-life means roughly 5.5% of a tritium inventory converts to helium-3 each year. This is slow and steady — an advantage for supply planning, because the conversion cannot run away or stall. A tritium store put aside today is a predictable helium-3 store tomorrow. It also means helium-3 accumulates whether or not any machine is running, so the breeder can build a helium-3 reserve before the first burner needs it.
Decay energy low (≤18.6 keV), no gamma emission
Conversion is passive and predictable — good for inventory planning
This decay is the single physical fact that makes a terrestrial helium-3 supply possible at all. Every other terrestrial source of helium-3 traces back to the same process happening somewhere else.

title: The Breeder–Burner Link
lede: The breeder makes the helium-3 the burner needs; the burner gives the breeder's helium-3 a purpose — a deliberately coupled two-machine system.
body: Kronos does not treat the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) as separate products that happen to share a company. They are engineered as a coupled system. The breeder is a source of tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons; the burner is a consumer of helium-3 and a producer of firm electric power. Neither is complete without the other: a burner with no helium-3 source cannot be fielded at scale, and a breeder with no helium-3 customer under-uses one of its products.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 165" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">COUPLED SYSTEM</text><rect x="40" y="55" width="180" height="70" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="130.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">BREEDER (Hyperion)</text><text x="130.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">source: T, <sup>3</sup>He, neutrons</text><line x1="224" y1="80" x2="436" y2="80" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="330.0" y="74.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">helium-3</text><line x1="436" y1="105" x2="224" y2="105" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="4 3" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="330" y="122" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">demand signal · fleet planning</text><rect x="440" y="55" width="180" height="70" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="530.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">BURNER (Aegis)</text><text x="530.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">consumer: firm power</text></svg>

The link also sets the build order. The breeder is built first because it makes the fuel: construction begins Q2 2027 and first-of-a-kind first tritium is expected around 2030. Helium-3 then accumulates by decay while the burner is still being perfected on paper and in simulation. The first test burner follows around 2032. By the time burners are fielded in numbers, a breeder fleet is intended to be running ahead of them as the fuel foundry.
Breeder is the fuel source; burner is the fuel consumer
Build order: breeder first, then test burner (~2032)
Helium-3 reserve accumulates by decay during the gap
Fleet planning couples breeder count to burner demand

This is why the burner's fuel supply is presented honestly as a design-stage story. The physics of the link is settled; the hardware is being built in the right order to make it real, and no step claims a net-gain result that has not been shown.

title: Deuterium Supply
lede: Deuterium, the burner's other fuel, is a stable isotope of hydrogen extracted from ordinary water and available in effectively unlimited quantity.
body: The easy half of the fuel

Deuterium (<sup>2</sup>H or D) is a stable, naturally occurring isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron. It makes up about 156 parts per million of all hydrogen on Earth, which means every litre of ordinary water contains a small but recoverable amount. Because the oceans hold an enormous mass of hydrogen, the practical supply of deuterium is effectively inexhaustible and is not a strategic or scarce material.

Deuterium is concentrated by well-established industrial processes. Chemical exchange (such as the Girdler sulfide process) and water distillation enrich water in the heavier HDO and D<sub>2</sub>O forms; electrolysis then liberates deuterium gas. These are mature technologies used for decades to make heavy water for other purposes. Nothing about Aegis requires a new deuterium industry — only access to an existing one.
Extracted from water by exchange, distillation, and electrolysis
Supply is effectively unlimited and non-strategic

This is why the burner's fuel-security conversation is really a helium-3 conversation. Deuterium is the reliable, abundant partner; the scarce, bred partner is helium-3. The two are stored, conditioned, and injected together, but their supply chains could not be more different.

title: Helium-3 Scarcity
lede: Helium-3 is one of the rarest usable isotopes on Earth; its scarcity is the central fact the breeder–burner pairing is designed to overcome.
body: Helium-3 makes up only about 1.38 parts per million of natural helium, and helium itself is a trace gas. There is no ore, no mine, and no large natural reservoir of pure helium-3 on Earth. Almost all terrestrial helium-3 in use today comes from the decay of tritium that was itself manufactured — historically in nuclear weapons programs. Because that tritium production has largely stopped, the existing supply is a slowly shrinking legacy stock.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">TERRESTRIAL HELIUM-3</text><rect x="40" y="60" width="580" height="30" fill="none" stroke="#3A4756" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="40" y="60" width="2.5" height="30" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="52" y="80" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11"><sup>3</sup>He ≈ 1.38 ppm of helium</text><text x="40" y="118" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">No ore. No mine. Supply = whatever tritium has decayed somewhere.</text><text x="40" y="138" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Sources: weapons-tritium decay (declining), natural-gas traces, and — deliberately — a fusion breeder.</text></svg>
Why scarcity is the design problem

Any programme that wants to burn D–<sup>3</sup>He at scale runs straight into this wall: there simply is not enough helium-3 in circulation to fuel a fleet of generators. Some proposals answer this by looking to the Moon, where solar wind has implanted helium-3 in the regolith over billions of years. Kronos treats lunar helium-3 as a genuine long-term supplement, not a near-term dependency.
Abundance ~1.38 ppm of a trace gas — no natural reservoir
Legacy supply is decaying weapons tritium — and it is shrinking
Demand from quantum, medical, and security uses already competes
A fusion breeder is a purpose-built, renewable terrestrial source

The breeder is Kronos's answer to scarcity. Instead of competing for a fixed legacy stock, Hyperion manufactures fresh tritium that decays into helium-3, turning a scarce isotope into a produced one. That is what makes a burner fleet conceivable at all.

title: Helium-3 Inventory Management
lede: Because helium-3 arrives slowly by decay, the supply is managed as an inventory — a reserve built ahead of demand rather than produced on demand.
body: Helium-3 cannot be produced faster by turning a dial: it appears at the fixed rate set by tritium's 12.32-year half-life. That makes helium-3 supply an inventory-management problem. The breeder builds a tritium store, a chosen fraction is allowed to decay, and the resulting helium-3 is accumulated as a reserve. Burners draw down that reserve. The system is planned around stock and flow, not instantaneous production.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 185" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">STOCK BUILDS AHEAD OF DEMAND</text><polyline points="40,140 140,128 240,110 340,86 440,60 560,40" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="40" y1="150" x2="620" y2="150" stroke="#3A4756"/><line x1="40" y1="150" x2="40" y2="40" stroke="#3A4756"/><text x="330" y="172" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">time → (breeder running)</text><text x="20" y="95" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10" transform="rotate(-90 20 95)"><sup>3</sup>He reserve</text><line x1="360" y1="40" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="366" y="52" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10">first burner draw</text></svg>

Three levers set the helium-3 reserve. First, how many breeders run and at what tritium breeding ratio (the lever spans 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8). Second, what fraction of bred tritium is held for decay versus sold or used directly as tritium. Third, the timing — because decay is passive, starting the breeder early (construction from Q2 2027) means a reserve exists before the first test burner around 2032.
Supply rate is fixed by half-life — plan by stock and flow
Reserve is built ahead of demand, during the breeder-first period
Tritium-held vs helium-3-decayed split is an inventory decision
Breeding-ratio lever (1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8) scales the source rate

Managed this way, the slowness of decay becomes a strength: the supply is predictable years in advance and cannot be disrupted by a single event, because most of the future helium-3 already exists as tritium in store.

title: Fuel Storage and Handling
lede: Deuterium and helium-3 are light, non-corrosive gases stored cryogenically or as hydrides; helium-3 handling is dominated by containment against loss, not radiation.
body: The burner's two fuels are both light gases, but they are handled differently. Deuterium is a hydrogen isotope and can be stored as compressed gas, as a cryogenic liquid, or absorbed in metal hydride beds that release it on gentle heating. Helium-3 is a noble gas — chemically inert, non-radioactive, and impossible to store as a hydride — so it is kept as compressed or cryogenic gas in leak-tight vessels.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="6" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="66.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Metal hydride</text><text x="66.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">D₂ storage</text><line x1="128" y1="69.0" x2="150" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="152" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="212.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Cryo / compressed</text><text x="212.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5"><sup>3</sup>He storage</text><line x1="274" y1="69.0" x2="296" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="298" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="358.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Conditioning</text><text x="358.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">mix & purity</text><line x1="420" y1="69.0" x2="442" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="444" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="504.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Injection</text><text x="504.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">central cell</text></svg>
The dominant concern: loss, not exposure

Helium-3 itself is not a radiological hazard — it is stable and inert. The governing concern in its handling is preventing loss. Because it is scarce and bred at a fixed rate, an accidental venting is a supply loss that cannot be quickly replaced. Systems therefore emphasize leak-tight, double-contained vessels, helium-3-specific leak detection, and closed transfer. The radiological handling that does exist sits on the breeder side, around the tritium that helium-3 comes from.
Deuterium: compressed gas, cryogenic liquid, or metal-hydride beds
Helium-3: leak-tight compressed or cryogenic gas (inert, no hydride)
Helium-3 handling optimizes against loss, not against exposure
Tritium's radiological handling is a breeder-side concern
This split keeps the burner's on-site radiological inventory small. Aegis stores and burns a mostly-clean fuel; the more demanding tritium handling stays where the tritium is made.

title: Tritium Handling and Safety
lede: Tritium handling is a breeder-side discipline; because the burner's helium-3 comes from decayed tritium, tritium safety underpins the whole supply chain.
body: Tritium is the one radioactive isotope in the breeder–burner fuel story. It is a low-energy beta emitter — its radiation cannot penetrate skin — but it is a hazard if inhaled or ingested, and it is highly mobile because it behaves chemically like hydrogen and can permeate metals. Handling it safely is a mature engineering discipline: multiple containment barriers, tritium-compatible materials, atmosphere detritiation systems, and continuous monitoring.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">CONTAINMENT (BREEDER SIDE)</text><rect x="40" y="55" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="105.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Bred T</text><text x="105.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">primary barrier</text><rect x="200" y="55" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="265.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Secondary</text><text x="265.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">glovebox / vault</text><rect x="360" y="55" width="130" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="425.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Detritiation</text><text x="425.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">room air cleanup</text><rect x="520" y="55" width="110" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="575.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Monitor</text><text x="575.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">continuous</text><text x="330" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Multiple barriers keep bred tritium contained until it decays to inert helium-3.</text></svg>
Why it matters to the burner

The burner does not use tritium as a primary fuel, so a fielded Aegis site carries a much smaller radiological inventory than the breeder. But the burner's fuel supply is built on tritium: the helium-3 it burns is what tritium becomes. Reliable, safe tritium handling on the breeder side is therefore a precondition for the burner's fuel to exist at all. When tritium is held for decay, safe long-term containment is the mechanism that converts it to helium-3.
Tritium is a low-energy beta emitter — internal hazard, mobile
Handled by layered containment, detritiation, and monitoring
Burner site inventory is small; the tritium work is breeder-side
Safe long-term containment is how held tritium becomes helium-3
In short, the fuel loop trades a demanding-but-mature tritium discipline at the breeder for a clean fuel at the burner. The safety burden is concentrated where the expertise and infrastructure sit.
related: No Tritium Fuel in the Burner

title: Helium-3 Purity Requirements
lede: Fusion-grade helium-3 must be separated from ordinary helium-4 and other gases; even small contamination changes plasma behavior and fuel accounting.
body: The burner plasma is tuned to a specific fuel mix. Contaminants dilute the reacting species, radiate energy away, and shift the plasma's effective charge. Helium-4 is the chief concern: it is chemically identical to helium-3 and cannot be removed by chemistry, only by isotope separation. Other light gases — residual hydrogen, deuterium, nitrogen — must also be held to low levels. Purity is specified because impurities cost confinement and confuse fuel accounting.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 185" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">PURITY = SEPARATION</text><rect x="60" y="55" width="80" height="90" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="100" y="105" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13"><sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="100" y="160" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">wanted</text><line x1="150" y1="100" x2="230" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="190.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">reject</text><rect x="240" y="70" width="70" height="26" fill="none" stroke="#6E7D8F"/><text x="275" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5"><sup>4</sup>He</text><rect x="240" y="104" width="70" height="26" fill="none" stroke="#6E7D8F"/><text x="275" y="122" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5">H₂ / D₂</text><text x="360" y="105" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">Only isotope separation removes <sup>4</sup>He.</text></svg>

Helium-3 from tritium decay is intrinsically clean at birth, but it accumulates alongside the parent tritium and any helium-4 already present, and it can pick up gases during storage and transfer. Recovered helium-3 from a burner's exhaust is mixed with the helium-4 ash the reaction produces. So purity is maintained by separation both upstream (before delivery) and downstream (in exhaust processing).
Helium-4 dilutes fuel and cannot be removed chemically
Impurities radiate energy and raise effective charge
Decay-born helium-3 is clean but co-located with tritium and <sup>4</sup>He
Purity is enforced by isotope separation, upstream and downstream
Specifying and verifying purity is therefore tied directly to the isotope-separation and fuel-accounting systems described elsewhere in this section.

title: Isotope Separation
lede: Separating helium-3 from helium-4 relies on their small mass difference, using cryogenic distillation and related physical methods rather than chemistry.
body: Helium-3 and helium-4 are the same element, so no chemical reaction can tell them apart. They differ only in mass — three versus four nucleons — and separation exploits that difference physically. The principal method is cryogenic distillation: at temperatures near the boiling point of helium, the lighter helium-3 is slightly more volatile and concentrates in the vapor. Repeated stages enrich it to fusion grade.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 185" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">CRYOGENIC DISTILLATION</text><rect x="150" y="40" width="60" height="120" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="180" y="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">column</text><text x="180" y="58" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11"><sup>3</sup>He rich</text><text x="180" y="150" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11"><sup>4</sup>He rich</text><line x1="120" y1="100" x2="148" y2="60" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="120" y1="100" x2="148" y2="140" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="60" y="103" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10.5">He feed</text><line x1="212" y1="55" x2="300" y2="55" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="256.0" y="49.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">product</text><text x="310" y="58" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">fusion-grade <sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="310" y="150" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">vent / reuse <sup>4</sup>He</text></svg>

Besides distillation, the mass difference can be exploited by superfluid and phase-separation effects at very low temperature, and by diffusion and thermal-gradient methods. In practice a fusion fuel plant combines coarse bulk separation with fine polishing stages to reach the required helium-3 purity. The energy and hardware cost of separation is why purity specifications are set no tighter than the plasma actually needs.
No chemical route — separation is purely physical
Cryogenic distillation is the primary method
Superfluid, diffusion, and thermal methods supplement it

Separation appears twice in the fuel cycle: upstream, when decay-born helium-3 is cleaned of helium-4 before delivery, and downstream, when helium-3 is recovered from burner exhaust that is full of helium-4 ash.

title: The Fuel Injection System
lede: Fuel enters the central cell as gas or frozen pellets, replacing what the plasma burns and controlling density and the deuterium–helium-3 ratio in real time.
body: A burning plasma consumes fuel and must be continuously refuelled. In the tandem mirror the reacting plasma lives in the central cell, so that is where fuel is delivered. Two methods are used together: gas puffing, which admits neutral gas at the plasma edge, and pellet injection, which fires small frozen pellets deep into the plasma where the density is highest. Gas puffing is fast and fine; pellets place fuel where edge fuelling cannot reach.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 175" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">REFUELLING THE CENTRAL CELL</text><rect x="120" y="80" width="420" height="40" rx="20" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="330" y="105" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">central cell plasma</text><line x1="60" y1="70" x2="120" y2="88" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="90.0" y="73.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">pellet</text><line x1="60" y1="130" x2="120" y2="112" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="90.0" y="115.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">gas puff</text><circle cx="90" cy="100" r="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="560" y="104" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">density & D:<sup>3</sup>He control</text></svg>

Injection is a control system, not merely a feed pipe. By adjusting the rate and location of gas and pellets, operators set the plasma density and hold the deuterium-to-helium-3 ratio at its target. Because the two fuels burn at different rates and helium-3 is the scarce one, precise, well-metered injection is directly tied to fuel economy: over-feeding helium-3 wastes a bred resource, under-feeding it cools the burn.
Gas puffing: fast edge fuelling and fine density trim
Pellet injection: deep fuelling where edge gas cannot reach
Injection sets both density and the D:<sup>3</sup>He ratio
Metering helium-3 precisely is a fuel-economy requirement

The injection system is instrumented and closed-loop, tied to the density and composition diagnostics so the fuel mix stays on target through the burn. It is one of the main places the burner's control brain touches the fuel supply.

title: The Deuterium–Helium-3 Mix Ratio
lede: The ratio of deuterium to helium-3 sets the balance between fusion power and neutron production, and is chosen to keep the neutron fraction low.
body: A dial between power and cleanliness

The fuel mix is not simply one-to-one. The deuterium-to-helium-3 ratio is a design choice with a real trade-off. More deuterium raises the rate of D–D and D–T side reactions, which increases neutron output; more helium-3 favors the clean primary channel but demands more of the scarce isotope and higher temperatures to burn. The Aegis design point places this ratio where the neutron fraction settles at 5.44% of fusion power.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">THE MIX-RATIO TRADE-OFF</text><line x1="60" y1="120" x2="600" y2="120" stroke="#3A4756"/><text x="60" y="145" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">more D → more neutrons</text><text x="600" y="145" text-anchor="end" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">more <sup>3</sup>He → cleaner, harder</text><circle cx="300" cy="120" r="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><line x1="300" y1="60" x2="300" y2="110" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/><text x="300" y="52" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">Aegis design point · f_n = 5.44%</text></svg>

In principle pushing the mix toward pure helium-3 would minimize neutrons. In practice this raises the required temperature and the helium-3 demand, and a mirror plasma still contains deuterium that reacts with itself regardless. The chosen ratio is a balance: low enough neutron fraction to keep the machine clean and long-lived, while remaining reachable in the tandem-mirror configuration and economical in its use of bred helium-3.
Ratio trades fusion power against neutron production
Excess deuterium raises D–D and D–T neutron channels
Excess helium-3 is cleaner but harder to burn and scarcer
Design point: neutron fraction 5.44% at the chosen ratio

Because the ratio is set by injection, it is maintained actively during the burn. Diagnostics track the actual in-plasma composition and the control system trims injection to hold the target — the mix ratio is enforced, not assumed.

title: D–D Side Reactions
lede: Deuterium reacting with itself is the main source of neutrons in the burner; understanding these side channels explains the 5.44% neutron fraction.
body: Even in a fuel optimized for the clean D–<sup>3</sup>He channel, deuterium nuclei collide with each other. The D–D reaction has two branches of nearly equal probability: D + D → T + p, and D + D → <sup>3</sup>He + n (2.45 MeV neutron). The first branch produces tritium, which then reacts with deuterium (D + T → <sup>4</sup>He + n) to release a 14.1 MeV neutron. These are the channels that keep the burner from being perfectly aneutronic.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">D–D BRANCHES AND FOLLOW-ON</text><rect x="40" y="50" width="120" height="50" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="100.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D + D</text><line x1="164" y1="60" x2="240" y2="50" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="244" y="30" width="150" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="319.0" y="44.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">T + p</text><text x="319.0" y="62.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">branch A</text><line x1="164" y1="90" x2="240" y2="110" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="244" y="90" width="180" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="334.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600"><sup>3</sup>He + n (2.45 MeV)</text><text x="334.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">branch B</text><line x1="320" y1="70" x2="410" y2="70" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="430" y="50" width="180" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="520.0" y="64.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D+T→<sup>4</sup>He+n (14.1 MeV)</text><text x="520.0" y="82.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">follow-on</text></svg>

Adding up the neutron-producing channels — the D–D branch that makes a neutron directly, plus the D–T reaction fed by the tritium from the other branch — against the total fusion power gives the neutron fraction. At the Aegis design point this sums to 5.44%. It is a computed consequence of the fuel mix and plasma conditions, not a target set independently. Change the mix or the temperature and the fraction moves.
D–D branch A: D + D → T + p
D–D branch B: D + D → <sup>3</sup>He + n (2.45 MeV)
Sum of neutron channels / total power = 5.44%

One useful by-product: branch A and branch B both make useful fuel — tritium and helium-3 — inside the burner itself. This does not close the fuel cycle (the amounts are small and the burn consumes far more helium-3 than it makes), but it is a real, if minor, internal contribution.

title: Neutron Fraction and Fuel Choice
lede: The 5.44% neutron fraction is the honest cost of running D–3He in a real plasma, and it shapes shielding, materials, and maintenance.
body: Marketing a fusion fuel as aneutronic invites the assumption that it produces no neutrons. That is not true for D–<sup>3</sup>He in a real device, and Aegis does not claim it. The design point carries a neutron fraction of 5.44% of total fusion power — a large reduction from D–T's roughly 80%, but a real number that the machine is engineered around. Being honest about it is what lets the shielding and materials be sized correctly.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 135" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">NEUTRON FRACTION, HONESTLY</text><rect x="60" y="60" width="240" height="34" fill="none" stroke="#6E7D8F"/><rect x="60" y="60" width="192" height="34" fill="#6E7D8F" opacity="0.35"/><text x="60" y="112" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">D–T: ~80% of power as neutrons</text><rect x="360" y="60" width="240" height="34" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="360" y="60" width="13" height="34" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="360" y="112" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">D–<sup>3</sup>He (Aegis): 5.44%</text></svg>

The low fraction is why Aegis suits fixed installations: less neutron flux means less activation of structures, lighter shielding than a D–T machine of similar output, longer component life, and a smaller waste and maintenance burden. But 5.44% is not nothing. It still requires neutron shielding, activation-aware material choices, and a maintenance plan. The design treats the neutron fraction as a real engineering input rather than rounding it to zero.
5.44% vs ~80% for D–T — a large but incomplete reduction
Enables lighter shielding and longer component life
Still requires shielding and activation-aware materials
Sized from the honest number, not an idealized claim

The fuel choice and the neutron fraction are inseparable. Choosing D–<sup>3</sup>He is choosing a machine whose whole shielding, materials, and maintenance philosophy follows from 5.44% — and choosing to plan a helium-3 supply to feed it.

title: Fuel-Cycle Closure
lede: The burner's fuel cycle is deliberately open: it consumes bred helium-3 and returns helium-4 ash, and closure is achieved only at the two-machine system level.
body: The burner does not close its own cycle

A D–T reactor is often designed to breed its own tritium and approach self-sufficiency. The burner is different, and honestly so: it consumes helium-3 and deuterium and produces helium-4 ash plus power. Its internal side reactions make a trace of tritium and helium-3, but far less than it burns. On its own, the burner's fuel cycle is open — it is a net consumer of helium-3.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 165" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">OPEN AT THE MACHINE, CLOSED AT THE SYSTEM</text><rect x="40" y="60" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Breeder</text><text x="115.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">makes <sup>3</sup>He</text><line x1="192" y1="90" x2="270" y2="90" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="231.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10"><sup>3</sup>He</text><rect x="274" y="60" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="349.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Burner</text><text x="349.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">burns D+<sup>3</sup>He</text><line x1="426" y1="90" x2="504" y2="90" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="465.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10"><sup>4</sup>He ash</text><rect x="508" y="60" width="120" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="568.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Exhaust</text><text x="568.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">+ power</text><text x="330" y="145" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Closure exists at the SYSTEM level, not inside the burner.</text></svg>

Where closure does apply is across the breeder–burner system. The breeder manufactures helium-3 from bred tritium; the burner consumes it. Deuterium is drawn from an effectively unlimited external source. Helium-4 ash is exhausted, and any helium-3 not fully burned is recovered and recycled. The loop that matters — helium-3 in, helium-4 out — is balanced by production at the breeder, not by breeding inside the burner.
Burner is a net helium-3 consumer — cycle open at the machine
Products: helium-4 ash, power, trace T and <sup>3</sup>He
System closes when breeder production matches burner demand

Framing closure honestly is important: it makes clear why the breeder is not optional. The burner cannot be run at scale without a matching helium-3 source, which is precisely the breeder's role in the coupled system.

title: The Tritium Breeding Ratio Lever
lede: In the breeder, the tritium breeding ratio is a design lever spanning 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 — and it directly sets how fast helium-3 can be supplied.
body: The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) measures how many tritium atoms the breeder's blanket produces per tritium atom consumed in its D–T reaction. Hyperion treats TBR as a design lever explored across three values: 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8. A higher ratio means more surplus tritium beyond what the breeder needs to sustain itself — and that surplus is exactly what decays into the helium-3 the burner runs on.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 185" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">BREEDING-RATIO LEVER</text><rect x="80" y="120" width="100" height="30" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.5" stroke="#D4AD5C"/><text x="130" y="167" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">TBR 1.1</text><rect x="280" y="80" width="100" height="70" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.5" stroke="#D4AD5C"/><text x="330" y="167" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">TBR 1.5</text><rect x="480" y="45" width="100" height="105" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.5" stroke="#D4AD5C"/><text x="530" y="167" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">TBR 1.8</text><text x="40" y="40" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">surplus tritium → <sup>3</sup>He supply rate</text></svg>

It is important that TBR is presented as a lever, not as a single settled value. The physics of achieving a high, net-positive breeding ratio in a real blanket — including the difference between a local breeding figure and a whole-system net after losses — is an open engineering question that the breeder programme is designed to resolve. The three values bracket the plausible range; the helium-3 supply story scales with wherever it lands.
TBR = tritium atoms produced per atom consumed
Explored as a lever at 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8
Surplus above self-sufficiency becomes helium-3 by decay
Net vs local breeding is an open question the breeder resolves

For the burner, the practical reading is simple: the breeder's breeding-ratio choice is one of the main dials that sets how large and how fast the helium-3 reserve can grow, and therefore how many burners a breeder fleet can feed.

title: Helium-3 Yield from Hyperion
lede: At its design point the breeder yields helium-3 in the ~1.97 kg/yr class as bred tritium decays, alongside its ~4 kg/yr-class tritium output.
body: Hyperion's frozen design point pairs a tritium output in the ~4 kg/yr class with a helium-3 output in the ~1.97 kg/yr class. These are not two independent products so much as one material seen at two points in time: tritium is what the breeder makes, and helium-3 is what a portion of that tritium becomes as it decays on its 12.32-year clock.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">HYPERION DESIGN-POINT YIELDS</text><rect x="60" y="55" width="180" height="64" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Tritium</text><text x="150.0" y="99.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">~4 kg/yr class</text><line x1="244" y1="87" x2="360" y2="87" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="302.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">β decay over time</text><rect x="400" y="55" width="200" height="64" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="500.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Helium-3</text><text x="500.0" y="99.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">~1.97 kg/yr class</text><text x="330" y="150" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Plus ~14 MeV neutrons as a third product line.</text></svg>

These are per-unit, design-point figures for a single breeder at its reference operating condition. They scale with the number of breeders in the fleet and with the tritium breeding ratio chosen (the 1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8 lever). They are simulation and design outputs for a machine not yet built: construction begins Q2 2027 and first-of-a-kind first tritium is expected around 2030. No hardware net-gain result is claimed ahead of that milestone.
Tritium: ~4 kg/yr class per unit at the design point
Helium-3: ~1.97 kg/yr class per unit as tritium decays
Also produces 14 MeV neutrons as a third product
Design/simulation figures; first tritium ~2030, not yet built
For fleet planning the helium-3 figure is the one that governs how many burners a given number of breeders can feed. It is the throughput of the fuel foundry.

title: Tritium Yield from Hyperion
lede: The breeder's ~4 kg/yr-class tritium output is both a product in its own right and the reservoir from which the burner's helium-3 is drawn.
body: Hyperion's headline output is tritium — a design-point yield in the ~4 kg/yr class, produced when 14 MeV fusion neutrons breed tritium in a lithium-bearing blanket. Tritium is directly useful: it is a valuable isotope for the breeder line on its own terms. But for the burner it plays a second role, as the reservoir that decays into helium-3.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">TRITIUM PRODUCTION PATH</text><rect x="30" y="55" width="140" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="100.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Fusion n</text><text x="100.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">14 MeV</text><line x1="172" y1="84" x2="240" y2="84" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="244" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="319.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Li blanket</text><text x="319.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">breeds T</text><line x1="396" y1="84" x2="464" y2="84" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="430.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">T</text><rect x="468" y="55" width="160" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="548.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Tritium store</text><text x="548.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">~4 kg/yr class</text></svg>

Because tritium is both a saleable product and the precursor to helium-3, every unit of bred tritium poses a choice: use or sell it now as tritium, or hold it and let it become helium-3 for the burner. This split is an inventory decision set by fleet demand, and it is reversible in planning — tritium held for decay simply becomes helium-3 at the fixed half-life rate. The two product lines share one source stream.
~4 kg/yr-class tritium bred in a lithium blanket by 14 MeV neutrons
Tritium is a direct product and the helium-3 precursor
Held vs decayed split set by fleet demand
Understanding the tritium yield is therefore prerequisite to understanding helium-3 supply: helium-3 can never exceed what the tritium reservoir provides, and the reservoir's size is set here.

title: Supply Security
lede: Because both fuels are made domestically — deuterium from water, helium-3 from a home-built breeder — the burner's fuel supply is sovereign and resistant to disruption.
body: A fixed installation's power is only as resilient as its fuel. Fuels that must be imported, mined, or bought on a contested market are a vulnerability. The burner's fuel avoids that: deuterium comes from ordinary water, and helium-3 is bred at home by the breeder rather than sourced from a scarce, competed-for global stock. Both inputs are domestic, which is the technical meaning of sovereign power in the Aegis context.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">SOVEREIGN FUEL LOOP</text><rect x="40" y="55" width="160" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="120.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Water</text><text x="120.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">→ deuterium</text><rect x="250" y="55" width="160" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Home breeder</text><text x="330.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">→ helium-3</text><line x1="202" y1="85" x2="248" y2="85" stroke="#3A4756" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="412" y1="85" x2="470" y2="85" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="441.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">fuel</text><rect x="474" y="55" width="160" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="554.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Aegis</text><text x="554.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">firm power</text><text x="330" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">No import, no mine, no contested market in the loop.</text></svg>

Security comes from several features acting together. The helium-3 reserve is built ahead of demand, so most future fuel already exists in store. Deuterium is effectively unlimited. The breeder can be sited within the same jurisdiction as the burners it feeds. And because helium-3 arrives by slow decay, the supply is predictable years out and cannot be interrupted by a single event upstream.
Both fuels are domestically produced — no import dependency
Helium-3 reserve is pre-built, not produced on demand

This is a design-stage promise resting on a built breeder. The security is real only once the breeder fleet exists and is producing — which is why the programme builds the breeder first and treats lunar helium-3 as a supplement, not a crutch.

title: Lunar Helium-3 as a Long-Term Supplement
lede: The Moon holds solar-wind helium-3 in its regolith; Kronos treats it as a genuine long-term supplement to breeder-made helium-3, not a near-term dependency.
body: For billions of years the solar wind has streamed helium-3 into the Moon's surface, implanting it in the regolith. With no atmosphere or magnetic field to deflect it, the Moon has accumulated helium-3 that Earth largely lacks. Concentrations are low — parts per billion by mass — so recovery means heating large volumes of regolith, but the total resource is large and, unlike Earth's legacy tritium stock, it is not shrinking.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">LUNAR RESOURCE</text><circle cx="140" cy="100" r="55" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="140" y="104" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12">Moon</text><line x1="240" y1="30" x2="222" y2="70" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="270" y1="30" x2="252" y2="70" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="300" y1="30" x2="282" y2="70" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="330" y1="30" x2="312" y2="70" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="360" y1="30" x2="342" y2="70" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1"/><text x="300" y="24" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5">solar wind → implanted <sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="240" y="140" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">Regolith: ppb-level, but vast and not declining.</text></svg>

Lunar helium-3 is a real long-term supplement, but it is not the near-term supply. Recovering it requires lunar surface operations and transport that do not yet exist, and the programme deliberately does not depend on them. The breeder is the primary, proven-in-principle terrestrial source. Lunar helium-3 becomes relevant only later, as a way to expand supply beyond what a breeder fleet alone can produce, on a horizon of roughly the late 2030s and beyond.
Solar wind implants helium-3 in lunar regolith over billions of years
Concentrations are ppb-level but the total resource is large
Recovery needs lunar operations that do not yet exist
A long-term supplement to breeder helium-3, not a near-term crutch
The honest framing matters: the burner's fuel case stands on the breeder alone. Lunar helium-3 is upside, sequenced far behind the terrestrial supply, and nothing in the near-term plan assumes it.

title: The Fuel Supply Chain, End to End
lede: From water and lithium at the breeder to a burning plasma at the installation, the fuel supply chain has a small number of well-defined links.
body: The whole chain in one view

The burner's fuel chain is short and mostly domestic. On the deuterium side: water is enriched to heavy water and electrolyzed to deuterium gas. On the helium-3 side: the breeder breeds tritium from lithium using fusion neutrons, the tritium is held and decays to helium-3, and the helium-3 is separated from helium-4 to fusion grade. Both fuels are then stored, conditioned to the target mix, and injected into the central cell.

Two features stand out. First, the deuterium branch is short and industrial; the helium-3 branch runs through the breeder and is the longer, slower, more valuable path. Second, separation appears on the helium-3 branch to guarantee purity before the fuel meets the deuterium stream. Downstream of injection, helium-4 ash and unburned helium-3 are removed in exhaust processing, with helium-3 recovered and returned to store.
Deuterium branch: water → heavy water → D<sub>2</sub> store (short, industrial)
Helium-3 branch: Li blanket → tritium → decay → separation (long, bred)
Streams meet at conditioning, set to the target D:<sup>3</sup>He ratio
Exhaust processing recovers unburned helium-3 downstream
Every link here is either mature industrial technology (deuterium, separation, storage) or the breeder itself. The chain has no step that depends on unproven mining or off-planet logistics.

title: Breeder Helium-3 vs Lunar Helium-3
lede: Breeder-made and lunar helium-3 are complementary sources with very different readiness; the breeder is the near-term supply and the Moon is later upside.
body: There are two credible ways to obtain helium-3 at scale: breed it on Earth via tritium decay, or recover it from lunar regolith. They yield the same isotope but differ sharply in readiness, infrastructure, and timing. Kronos's plan leans on the breeder first and treats the Moon as a later supplement, and the honest comparison below is why.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 165" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">COMPLEMENTARY, NOT COMPETING</text><rect x="60" y="60" width="220" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="170.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">BREEDER</text><text x="170.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">near-term, terrestrial</text><rect x="380" y="60" width="220" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="490.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">LUNAR</text><text x="490.0" y="102.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">long-term supplement</text><line x1="285" y1="90" x2="375" y2="90" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="330.0" y="84.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">sequence</text><text x="330" y="145" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Same isotope; the breeder de-risks the supply, the Moon expands it.</text></svg>
Why not skip to the Moon?

Lunar helium-3 is often proposed as the answer to scarcity, but building an off-planet supply chain before a single burner runs would couple the whole programme to lunar logistics that do not yet exist. The breeder avoids that: it is a terrestrial machine on a defined build schedule, and it makes helium-3 whether or not lunar operations ever mature. The Moon then becomes upside for fleet expansion, not a single point of failure.
Same product isotope from two very different sources
Breeder is buildable now and plannable by decay rate
Lunar recovery needs infrastructure that does not exist yet
The comparison is not breeder versus lunar as rivals. It is a sequence: prove and scale the terrestrial source, then add lunar supply on top when its logistics exist.

title: Deuterium from Heavy Water
lede: Deuterium is recovered by concentrating water into heavy water and electrolyzing it — mature processes that require no new industry for the burner.
body: Deuterium is bound up in water as HDO and, rarely, D<sub>2</sub>O. Concentrating it means preferentially enriching these heavier molecules. The Girdler sulfide process cycles water and hydrogen sulfide between hot and cold towers, using the temperature-dependent tendency of deuterium to shift between the two, to progressively enrich water in deuterium. Vacuum distillation and other exchange methods refine the product further to reactor-grade heavy water.

Heavy water is electrolyzed to release deuterium gas, which is dried, purified, and stored for the fuel plant. All of this is decades-old industrial practice — heavy water has been produced at scale for other purposes for generations. Aegis therefore adds no new deuterium-production technology; it draws on an existing, well-understood supply base. The only fuel-technology novelty on the burner side is helium-3 handling, not deuterium.
Deuterium enriched from water as HDO / D<sub>2</sub>O
Girdler sulfide process plus distillation to heavy water
Electrolysis releases deuterium gas for storage
Mature technology — no new deuterium industry required
This maturity is part of why the burner's fuel-security discussion focuses on helium-3: the deuterium half of the fuel is a solved, abundant, industrial commodity.

title: Fuel Accountancy
lede: Because helium-3 is scarce and bred, every gram is tracked through a mass-balance system spanning breeder, store, burner, and exhaust recovery.
body: When a fuel is abundant, you meter it; when a fuel is bred slowly and cannot be quickly replaced, you account for it. Helium-3 falls in the second category. A fuel-accountancy system maintains a mass balance across the whole loop: helium-3 produced at the breeder, held in store, injected into the burner, burned, and recovered from exhaust. The books must close — helium-3 in must equal helium-3 burned plus helium-3 returned plus known losses.

A closed mass balance does two jobs. Operationally, it tells the fleet how much helium-3 is available and how far the reserve can stretch, feeding the inventory-management plan. It also provides material accountancy: because helium-3 comes from tritium, the same discipline that tracks a strategic, bred isotope for supply purposes supports the safeguards and reporting expected of any tritium-derived material.
Mass balance across breeder, store, burner, and exhaust
Books must close: in = burned + recovered + losses
Feeds inventory management and fleet planning
Supports safeguards for a tritium-derived material

Accurate accountancy depends on the fuel-cycle instrumentation — flow, composition, and inventory measurements at each node — which is why measurement and accounting are treated together in this section.

title: Fuel Recycling in the Central Cell
lede: Most helium-3 is not burned in a single pass; recovering and recycling the unburned fraction is essential to using a scarce fuel efficiently.
body: A fuel atom injected into the plasma has a probability of reacting before it leaves; the fraction that actually burns per pass is well below one. For a scarce fuel like helium-3, letting the unburned remainder escape unrecovered would waste a bred resource. So the fuel cycle is built to recover unburned helium-3 (and deuterium) from the exhaust, clean it, and return it to the fuel stream.
