Exhaust from the burn is a mix of helium-4 ash, unburned helium-3 and deuterium, and trace species. Processing removes the helium-4 ash (by isotope separation) and any impurities, and returns clean helium-3 and deuterium to the store. Effective recycling multiplies the useful output of every gram the breeder makes: a fuel that is used many times over stretches a fixed supply much further than one burned once and lost.
Burn fraction per pass is well below one
Unburned helium-3 and deuterium are recovered from exhaust
Helium-4 ash and impurities are separated out
Recycling stretches a fixed, bred helium-3 supply

Recycling ties directly to fuel accountancy: the recovered fraction is one of the terms that must balance in the helium-3 mass ledger, and improving recovery is one of the levers for feeding more burners per breeder.

title: Exhaust and Ash Removal
lede: The burner's exhaust carries helium-4 ash and unburned fuel out through the mirror ends; processing it removes ash and returns fuel to the loop.
body: In a tandem mirror, particles that are not confined stream out along the field lines through the end regions. This end loss, often a problem to be minimized, doubles as the exhaust path: helium-4 ash produced by the burn, along with unburned helium-3 and deuterium, leaves the central cell toward the expanders and end cells. The exhaust is collected there rather than at a divertor as in a tokamak.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">END-REGION EXHAUST</text><rect x="200" y="80" width="260" height="40" rx="20" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><text x="330" y="105" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="11">central cell</text><path d="M200 80 L120 55 L120 145 L200 120 Z" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.4"/><path d="M460 80 L540 55 L540 145 L460 120 Z" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.4"/><line x1="120" y1="100" x2="60" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="90.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">exhaust</text><line x1="540" y1="100" x2="600" y2="100" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="330" y="160" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">End loss becomes the exhaust and direct-conversion path.</text></svg>

The collected exhaust is pumped, cooled, and sent to fuel processing. There, helium-4 ash is separated from the valuable helium-3 and deuterium, impurities are removed, and the recovered fuel is returned to store. The helium-4 ash — inert and harmless — is the burner's main routine waste stream, and it is vented or collected without special radiological handling.
Exhaust exits along field lines through the mirror ends
Carries helium-4 ash plus unburned helium-3 and deuterium
Processing separates ash from recoverable fuel
Helium-4 ash is inert — the main routine waste stream

Because the exhaust path is also where charged particles are directed for direct energy conversion, exhaust handling and power conversion share the same end-region hardware — a point where the fuel cycle and the power cycle physically meet.

title: Helium-4 Ash Management
lede: Helium-4 is the burner's principal by-product: an inert, non-radioactive gas that must be removed from the plasma and separated from unburned helium-3.
body: The primary D–<sup>3</sup>He reaction produces a helium-4 nucleus (an alpha particle). As the burn proceeds, helium-4 accumulates in the plasma as ash. Unlike the activated waste of neutron-heavy reactors, helium-4 is completely inert and non-radioactive — the same gas used to fill balloons. The challenge it poses is not hazard but dilution: ash left in the plasma displaces fuel, radiates energy, and eventually would quench the burn.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 165" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">ASH ACCUMULATION</text><rect x="120" y="60" width="420" height="60" rx="30" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><circle cx="170" cy="90" r="6" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.6"/><circle cx="240" cy="90" r="6" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.6"/><circle cx="310" cy="90" r="6" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.6"/><circle cx="380" cy="90" r="6" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.6"/><circle cx="450" cy="90" r="6" fill="#D4AD5C" opacity="0.6"/><text x="330" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10.5"><sup>4</sup>He ash builds up → must be pumped out</text><line x1="500" y1="120" x2="560" y2="140" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="530.0" y="124.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">remove</text></svg>

Ash is removed with the end-region exhaust and then separated from the unburned helium-3 it is mixed with. Because helium-3 and helium-4 differ only in mass, this is the same isotope-separation step used to purify incoming fuel — done here in reverse, to reclaim helium-3 and discard the helium-4. The recovered helium-3 returns to store; the helium-4 is collected or vented as an inert, ordinary waste.
Primary reaction produces helium-4 (alpha) as ash
Ash is inert and non-radioactive — a handling non-issue
Must be removed to prevent fuel dilution and radiation losses
Separated from unburned helium-3 by isotope separation

The cleanliness of the ash is one of the burner's clearest advantages for fixed installations: the routine by-product of operation is a harmless gas, not activated material, which is why the design suits low-signature, sited power.

title: Fuelling Rate and Burn Fraction
lede: The rate fuel is injected and the fraction that burns per pass together set how much helium-3 a burner consumes to hold a given power.
body: Helium-3 demand at an installation follows from two quantities. The fuelling rate is how fast fresh and recycled fuel must be injected to sustain the plasma density against burn and loss. The burn fraction is what proportion of injected fuel reacts before leaving. A low burn fraction means fuel must be cycled many times, which raises the importance of recovery; the fuelling rate then sets the throughput the fuel plant must handle.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 145" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">SIZING HELIUM-3 DEMAND</text><text x="20" y="46" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="12">net <sup>3</sup>He use = injected × (1 − recovery of unburned)</text><rect x="20" y="70" width="150" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="95.0" y="86.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Fuelling rate</text><text x="95.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">injection</text><rect x="200" y="70" width="150" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="275.0" y="86.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Burn fraction</text><text x="275.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">per pass</text><line x1="355" y1="92" x2="415" y2="92" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="385.0" y="86.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">× recovery</text><rect x="430" y="70" width="180" height="44" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="520.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Net <sup>3</sup>He demand</text></svg>

Because the per-pass burn fraction is well below one, most injected helium-3 is not consumed on any given pass — it leaves in the exhaust. If that fraction is recovered and recycled, the net consumption is small relative to the throughput. If it were not recovered, net consumption would balloon and no realistic breeder supply could keep up. This is why recycling is not an optimization but a requirement for a scarce, bred fuel.
Fuelling rate sustains plasma density against burn and loss
Burn fraction per pass is well below one
Net demand = injected minus recovered unburned fuel
High recovery keeps net helium-3 consumption low
For fleet planning, net helium-3 demand per burner is the figure that must be matched against the breeder's ~1.97 kg/yr-class output per unit to decide how many burners a breeder can feed.

title: Fuel Conditioning
lede: Before injection, deuterium and helium-3 are purified, dried, blended to the target ratio, and formed into the gas or pellets the plasma requires.
body: Fuel drawn from storage is not ready to inject as-is. Conditioning is the set of steps that turns stored gas into a plasma-ready feed. It removes residual impurities and moisture, verifies isotopic purity, blends deuterium and helium-3 to the target ratio, and prepares the physical form — clean gas for puffing, or frozen solid pellets for deep injection. Conditioning is where the fuel's chemistry and composition are finalized.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="6" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="66.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Purify</text><text x="66.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">remove impurities</text><line x1="128" y1="69.0" x2="150" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="152" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="212.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Verify</text><text x="212.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">isotopic purity</text><line x1="274" y1="69.0" x2="296" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="298" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="358.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Blend</text><text x="358.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">D : <sup>3</sup>He</text><line x1="420" y1="69.0" x2="442" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="444" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="504.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Form</text><text x="504.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">gas / pellet</text></svg>
Why conditioning is its own step

Separating conditioning from bulk storage keeps the large fuel inventory simple and stable while the exacting composition control happens on a small, active stream just before injection. It also places a final quality gate immediately upstream of the plasma: any off-spec fuel is caught here, not in the machine. For pellet fuelling, conditioning includes freezing and shaping the fuel to the size and speed the injector needs to place it deep in the plasma.
Verifies isotopic purity as a final gate
Blends deuterium and helium-3 to the target ratio
Forms gas for puffing or frozen pellets for deep injection
Conditioning connects storage, quality assurance, and injection into one continuous path, and it is instrumented so the composition delivered to the plasma is measured, not assumed.

title: Cryogenic Fuel Storage
lede: Storing fuel cold shrinks its volume and stabilizes it; helium-3, which cannot be stored as a hydride, is a prime candidate for cryogenic storage.
body: Light gases occupy large volumes at room temperature. Cooling them — to cryogenic liquid or dense cold gas — drastically reduces the volume a given quantity of fuel needs, and cold, sealed storage limits loss and contamination. Deuterium can be liquefied or absorbed in metal hydride beds, but helium-3 is a noble gas that forms no hydride, so cold storage in leak-tight vessels is its natural home.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 195" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">COLD STORAGE OF LIGHT FUELS</text><rect x="120" y="45" width="120" height="110" rx="10" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="180" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12"><sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="180" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">cryogenic</text><line x1="140" y1="160" x2="140" y2="175" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><line x1="160" y1="160" x2="160" y2="175" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><line x1="180" y1="160" x2="180" y2="175" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><line x1="200" y1="160" x2="200" y2="175" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><line x1="220" y1="160" x2="220" y2="175" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><rect x="380" y="45" width="120" height="110" rx="10" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="440" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="12">D₂</text><text x="440" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="9.5">liquid or hydride</text></svg>

Cryogenic storage requires vacuum-insulated vessels, refrigeration, and careful pressure and boil-off management. For helium-3 the paramount design goal remains loss prevention: because it is bred and scarce, boil-off and leaks are not just inefficiencies but supply losses. Vessels are double-contained and monitored, and boil-off is captured and re-liquefied rather than vented. The same cryogenic infrastructure supports the separation plant, since isotope separation of helium runs cold.
Cold storage shrinks volume and stabilizes light gases
Helium-3 forms no hydride — cryogenic or dense cold gas storage
Vacuum insulation, refrigeration, boil-off capture required
Loss prevention is the governing design goal for helium-3

Cryogenic storage, isotope separation, and dilution-refrigeration uses of helium-3 all share the same low-temperature engineering base, so the cold infrastructure serves multiple parts of the fuel system.

title: The Proton Product and Direct Conversion
lede: The 14.7 MeV proton from the primary reaction is a charged particle whose energy can be captured directly, linking the fuel choice to the burner's power path.
body: The reaction that pays off at the ends

The primary D–<sup>3</sup>He reaction sends most of its 18.3 MeV into a fast proton (14.7 MeV) and an alpha (3.6 MeV). Both are charged, and this is the crux of the fuel choice: charged products can be guided by magnetic and electric fields and their kinetic energy recovered by direct energy conversion, rather than only being turned into heat and then into electricity through a thermal cycle.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 175" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">CHARGED PRODUCT → DEC</text><rect x="40" y="70" width="150" height="56" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="92.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">D + <sup>3</sup>He</text><text x="115.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">primary burn</text><line x1="194" y1="98" x2="270" y2="98" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="232.0" y="92.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">p 14.7 MeV</text><path d="M280 70 L360 55 L360 141 L280 126 Z" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="320" y="102" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="10">expander</text><line x1="360" y1="98" x2="450" y2="98" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="454" y="70" width="170" height="56" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="539.0" y="92.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Direct converter</text><text x="539.0" y="110.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">charge → power</text></svg>
Why this is a fuel-supply topic

Direct conversion is usually filed under the power system, but it belongs to the fuel story too: it is the reason the burner tolerates the high cost of using helium-3. A fuel whose energy comes out as charged particles justifies the effort of breeding and handling a scarce isotope, because it converts to electricity more directly than a neutron-dominated fuel could. The fuel choice and the conversion method are two sides of the same design decision.
Primary products are charged: proton (14.7 MeV) and alpha (3.6 MeV)
Charged particles enable direct energy conversion
This justifies the cost of using scarce helium-3
Fuel choice and conversion method are one decision
The small neutron fraction (5.44%) is the part of the energy that cannot be directly converted and instead appears as heat and activation — another reason keeping that fraction low is valued.

title: No Tritium Fuel in the Burner
lede: Aegis does not use tritium as a primary fuel; it burns deuterium and helium-3, which keeps its on-site radiological inventory small.
body: Because tritium is central to the fuel story — it is what helium-3 is made from — it is easy to assume the burner runs on tritium. It does not. Aegis burns deuterium and helium-3. Tritium's role is upstream, at the breeder, as the precursor that decays into the helium-3 the burner uses. A fielded burner is not fuelled with tritium and does not need a tritium supply on site.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">TRITIUM STAYS UPSTREAM</text><rect x="30" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="105.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Breeder</text><text x="105.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">holds tritium</text><line x1="182" y1="84" x2="250" y2="84" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="216.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10"><sup>3</sup>He only</text><rect x="254" y="55" width="180" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="344.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Aegis site</text><text x="344.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">burns D + <sup>3</sup>He</text><line x1="182" y1="120" x2="254" y2="120" stroke="#6E7D8F" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="220" y="138" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">tritium stays at the breeder</text></svg>

Keeping tritium off the burner site is one reason Aegis suits fixed installations. Tritium is the fuel loop's one mobile radioactive species, demanding layered containment and detritiation wherever it lives. By confining that burden to the breeder and shipping only helium-3 — an inert, stable, non-radioactive gas — the burner carries a far smaller radiological footprint. A trace of tritium is generated internally by D–D side reactions, but this is a small in-machine quantity, not a fuel input.
Burner fuel is deuterium and helium-3, not tritium
Tritium's role is upstream, at the breeder
Helium-3 shipped to site is inert and non-radioactive
Only a trace of tritium arises internally, not as fuel

This separation of duties — radiological work at the breeder, clean fuel at the burner — is a deliberate feature of the two-machine system, and a large part of why the burner can be described as low-signature.

title: Helium-3 Transport and Logistics
lede: Moving helium-3 from breeder to burner means transporting a scarce, inert gas in leak-tight vessels, where the priority is preventing loss.
body: Helium-3 produced at the breeder must reach the installations that burn it. Transport is straightforward in principle — helium-3 is inert and non-radioactive, so it poses no radiological shipping hazard — but exacting in practice, because it is scarce and irreplaceable on a short timescale. The transported form is compressed or cryogenic gas in double-contained, leak-tight vessels, tracked as part of the fuel-accountancy ledger from the moment it leaves store.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">BREEDER → BURNER TRANSPORT</text><rect x="30" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="105.0" y="88.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Breeder store</text><line x1="182" y1="84" x2="270" y2="84" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="226.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="10">sealed vessel</text><rect x="274" y="55" width="120" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="334.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Transport</text><text x="334.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">leak-tight</text><line x1="396" y1="84" x2="484" y2="84" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="488" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="563.0" y="88.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Aegis store</text><text x="330" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Inert gas — no radiological shipping hazard; loss is the risk.</text></svg>

Because a leak is a permanent supply loss, transport hardware mirrors storage hardware: double containment, helium-specific leak detection, and monitored transfer at both ends. Chain-of-custody accounting means the same gram of helium-3 is on the books at the breeder store, in transit, and at the burner store, with reconciliations at each handoff. Co-locating breeders and burners within a jurisdiction shortens the logistics chain and strengthens supply security.
Helium-3 ships as inert compressed or cryogenic gas
No radiological shipping hazard — loss is the concern
Double containment, leak detection, monitored transfer

Transport is the physical link that turns the breeder's output into the burner's input, and it is governed by the same loss-prevention and accountancy discipline that runs through the whole helium-3 supply.

title: Fuel Quality Assurance
lede: Every batch of fuel is verified for isotopic purity and composition before it reaches the plasma, protecting both machine performance and the fuel ledger.
body: Fuel quality assurance is the set of checks that confirm what is about to be injected is actually what the plasma needs. It verifies isotopic purity — that helium-3 is not diluted with helium-4 — and confirms the deuterium-to-helium-3 blend and the absence of contaminant gases. Because off-spec fuel degrades confinement and confuses accounting, quality is checked as a gate, with out-of-tolerance batches diverted for reprocessing rather than injected.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><rect x="6" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="66.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Sample</text><text x="66.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">each batch</text><line x1="128" y1="69.0" x2="150" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="152" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="212.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Analyze</text><text x="212.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">isotopes + purity</text><line x1="274" y1="69.0" x2="296" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="298" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="358.0" y="63.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Pass?</text><text x="358.0" y="81.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">gate</text><line x1="420" y1="69.0" x2="442" y2="69.0" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><rect x="444" y="42" width="120" height="54" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="504.0" y="73.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Inject / reject</text></svg>

Analysis combines composition measurement (which isotopes and gases are present and in what proportion) with purity measurement (how much helium-4 and other contamination remains). Mass spectrometry and related techniques distinguish helium-3 from helium-4 despite their chemical identity. The results feed two systems at once: the plasma control system, which needs to know the exact mix it is fuelling, and the fuel-accountancy ledger, which needs to know the helium-3 content of every batch.
Verifies isotopic purity and the D:<sup>3</sup>He blend
Mass spectrometry distinguishes helium-3 from helium-4
Results feed both plasma control and fuel accounting

Quality assurance sits between conditioning and injection as the last checkpoint before the plasma, and it is what lets the composition delivered to the burn be a measured fact rather than an assumption.

title: Startup Fuel Inventory
lede: Bringing a burner online requires an initial helium-3 charge; this startup inventory is drawn from the reserve the breeder builds ahead of demand.
body: A burner cannot begin operating with an empty fuel store. It needs an initial helium-3 inventory large enough to fill the storage and conditioning systems, establish the recycle loop, and sustain the plasma while the recovery system reaches steady operation. This startup charge is a one-time draw on the helium-3 reserve, distinct from the ongoing consumption that recycling holds low.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">STARTUP VS STEADY DEMAND</text><polyline points="40,140 130,120 220,105 300,95" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="300" cy="95" r="5" fill="#D4AD5C"/><line x1="300" y1="95" x2="620" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="40" y1="150" x2="620" y2="150" stroke="#3A4756"/><text x="170" y="175" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10">startup charge (one-time draw)</text><text x="460" y="88" text-anchor="middle" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="10">steady-state (low, recycled)</text></svg>

The startup charge is exactly why the breeder is built first and the reserve accumulated ahead of demand. By the time the first test burner is ready around 2032, the breeder — running since roughly 2030 — should have built a helium-3 reserve from decayed tritium sufficient to charge it. Fleet growth is then paced by how quickly the reserve can supply successive startup charges plus the modest steady-state draw of the burners already running.
Startup requires a one-time helium-3 charge to fill the loop
Distinct from low, recycled steady-state consumption
Drawn from the reserve built during the breeder-first period
Fleet growth paced by reserve size and charge cadence

Planning the reserve therefore means summing all the startup charges for a planned burner fleet plus their running demand, and matching that against breeder production over time — the core calculation of the fuel-foundry model.

title: Steady-State Fuel Demand
lede: Once running and recycling, a burner's net helium-3 draw is small; steady-state demand is set by the unrecovered fraction, not the full throughput.
body: A common error is to equate a burner's helium-3 demand with the amount of fuel cycling through its plasma. Throughput is large — fuel is injected, mostly not burned per pass, and recovered. But net demand is only the part not returned to store: unburned fuel lost to imperfect recovery, plus the helium-3 actually consumed by fusion. With effective recycling, steady-state net demand is a small fraction of throughput.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 135" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">NET DEMAND IS A SLICE OF THROUGHPUT</text><rect x="60" y="60" width="360" height="34" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4"/><text x="60" y="112" fill="#9FB1C4" font-size="11">throughput (injected per pass)</text><rect x="60" y="60" width="46" height="34" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="440" y="82" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11">net demand = burned + unrecovered</text></svg>

Steady-state demand rises with the fusion power sustained (more burn consumes more fuel) and falls with better recovery efficiency (less unburned fuel lost). It does not depend on throughput directly. This is why recycling is treated as essential rather than optional: it is the lever that keeps net demand low enough for a breeder fleet to sustain many burners at once, rather than only a few.
Net demand = fuel burned + unrecovered unburned fuel
Independent of the much larger throughput
Rises with sustained power, falls with recovery efficiency
Low steady-state demand is what makes fleets feasible
Steady-state demand per burner, added to periodic startup charges, is what the fuel-accountancy and inventory systems track against the breeder's ~1.97 kg/yr-class output to plan the fleet.

title: Fuel Supply Redundancy
lede: Resilient power needs resilient fuel; redundancy comes from on-site reserves, multiple breeders, and the abundance of deuterium.
body: A fixed installation valued for resilience cannot depend on a single, fragile fuel path. The burner's fuel supply is made redundant in several independent ways so that no one disruption stops it. On-site helium-3 reserves buffer against interruptions upstream; multiple breeders mean production does not rest on one machine; and deuterium's abundance removes half the fuel from the risk picture entirely.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">LAYERS OF REDUNDANCY</text><rect x="40" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">On-site reserve</text><text x="115.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">buffer</text><rect x="255" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Multiple breeders</text><text x="330.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">no single source</text><rect x="470" y="55" width="150" height="58" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="545.0" y="78.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Abundant D</text><text x="545.0" y="96.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">never scarce</text><text x="330" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Independent layers — a disruption to one does not stop the burn.</text></svg>

Redundancy is strongest when the layers are independent. A local reserve covers short interruptions in delivery. A fleet of breeders covers the loss of any single production unit. The slow, predictable nature of decay-based supply means shortfalls appear gradually and can be managed, not suddenly. And because deuterium is effectively unlimited, only the helium-3 side needs this protection — halving the problem.
A breeder fleet removes single-source production risk
Slow decay supply gives early warning of any shortfall
Deuterium abundance removes half the fuel from risk

Redundancy is a design-stage commitment that becomes real as the breeder fleet grows. Until then it is planned into the fuel-foundry model, sizing reserves and breeder count to the resilience the installations require.

title: Deuterium Storage
lede: Deuterium is stored as compressed gas, cryogenic liquid, or metal hydride; its abundance makes storage a matter of convenience rather than scarcity.
body: Deuterium storage is comparatively relaxed. Unlike helium-3, deuterium is cheap to replace and effectively unlimited, so storage is chosen for operational convenience rather than to guard against loss. Three forms are common: compressed gas in cylinders, cryogenic liquid for high density, and metal hydride beds that absorb deuterium and release it on mild heating. Hydride storage is attractive because it holds a lot of fuel at low pressure and improves safety.

<svg viewBox="0 0 660 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:660px;height:auto;margin:14px 0;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/></marker></defs><text x="12" y="20" fill="#D4AD5C" font-size="11" letter-spacing="1.5">DEUTERIUM STORAGE OPTIONS</text><rect x="40" y="55" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="115.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Compressed</text><text x="115.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">cylinders</text><rect x="255" y="55" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#9FB1C4" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="330.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Cryogenic</text><text x="330.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">liquid D₂</text><rect x="470" y="55" width="150" height="60" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="545.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#E6ECF2" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Metal hydride</text><text x="545.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">low-pressure</text><text x="330" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6E7D8F" font-size="10.5">Chosen for convenience — deuterium is abundant and easily replaced.</text></svg>

Metal hydride storage deserves note because it is the deuterium option with no helium-3 equivalent. Certain metals absorb hydrogen isotopes into their crystal lattice, storing deuterium as a solid-bound gas at near-ambient pressure and releasing it when gently warmed. This gives compact, low-pressure, controllable storage that pairs well with the metered demands of fuel conditioning. Helium-3, being a noble gas, cannot be stored this way and must always be kept as gas.
Deuterium stored as compressed gas, cryogenic liquid, or hydride
Storage chosen for convenience, not loss prevention
Hydride beds hold much fuel at low pressure, safely
No hydride option exists for noble-gas helium-3
The contrast with helium-3 storage underlines the asymmetry of the fuel supply: one fuel is stored casually and the other guarded closely, reflecting which is abundant and which is bred.

title: Helium-3 in Global Context
lede: Today's helium-3 comes mainly from decaying weapons tritium and natural-gas traces, competed for by quantum, medical, and security uses — context for why a breeder matters.
body: Almost all helium-3 in use today traces to tritium decay, historically from tritium made in nuclear weapons programs, supplemented by tiny amounts recovered from natural gas. Because large-scale tritium production has largely ceased, this supply is a declining legacy stock. Meanwhile demand has grown: helium-3 is prized for ultra-low-temperature refrigeration (including cooling quantum-computer and detector systems), for neutron detection in security and science, and for medical lung imaging.

Why the breeder changes the picture

A fusion breeder is fundamentally different from these sources because it is a purpose-built, renewable producer rather than a shrinking legacy stock or a trace by-product. It makes fresh tritium that decays into fresh helium-3 for as long as it runs. This does not just supply the burner; it eases the broader helium-3 squeeze that other users face. The breeder turns helium-3 from a competed-for legacy commodity into a produced material.
Today: mostly decaying weapons tritium, plus natural-gas traces
Legacy supply is declining as tritium production has stopped
Demand from cryogenics, quantum, detection, and medicine
A breeder is a purpose-built, renewable source
This context is why the breeder–burner pairing is presented as the answer to scarcity: it does not compete for the existing pool, it enlarges it.

title: How a Breeder Fleet Feeds a Burner Fleet
lede: At scale, a fleet of breeders acts as a fuel foundry: each unit's helium-3 output supports a matched number of burners, sequenced breeder-first.
body: Scaled up, the two-machine system becomes a fleet relationship. A group of breeders functions as a fuel foundry, each producing helium-3 in the ~1.97 kg/yr class at its design point. That output, matched against the net steady-state demand and startup charges of the burners, determines how many burners the foundry can sustain. Growing the burner fleet requires growing the breeder fleet ahead of it, on the same breeder-first logic that governs the single-machine case.

Two rules govern the fleet. Sequencing: breeders come online first so a helium-3 reserve exists before burners need charging — construction from Q2 2027, first tritium ~2030, first test burner ~2032. Matching: the number of burners is bounded by breeder production, the breeding-ratio lever (1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8), recovery efficiency, and how much bred tritium is held for decay versus used directly. Lunar helium-3 could later raise the ceiling, but the near-term fleet is sized on terrestrial breeding alone.
Breeders act as a fuel foundry, each ~1.97 kg/yr class helium-3
Burner count bounded by breeder output and recovery efficiency
Breeder-first sequencing builds a reserve ahead of demand
Breeding-ratio lever scales how many burners a foundry feeds
This foundry model is the fleet-scale expression of the breeder–burner link: the same physics, planned across many machines, with the breeder always built ahead as the source of the burner's fuel.

title: Fuel Supply Risk and Mitigation
lede: The honest risks to the burner's fuel supply are breeder readiness, breeding ratio, and recovery efficiency — each with a defined mitigation.
body: A credible fuel plan states its risks. The burner's helium-3 supply depends on machines not yet built and on figures still being resolved, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The principal risks are the breeder's readiness on schedule, the tritium breeding ratio it actually achieves, the recovery efficiency the burner reaches, and any interruption to delivery. Each has a mitigation built into the programme's design and sequencing.
Breeder built first; reserve accrues before burners
Lever spans 1.1/1.5/1.8; plan to conservative end
Recycling engineered as a requirement, not option

The fuel supply is a design-stage plan, not a demonstrated capability. Its strongest guarantee is sequencing: by building the breeder first and letting a reserve accumulate by passive decay, the programme puts most of the burner's future fuel into store before any burner needs it. Uncertain figures like the breeding ratio are planned to their conservative end, and no step assumes lunar supply or a hardware net-gain result that has not been shown.
Risks: breeder readiness, breeding ratio, recovery, delivery
Mitigations: reserve, conservative planning, recycling, fleet depth
Sequencing puts fuel in store before it is needed
No reliance on lunar supply or unproven net-gain claims
Stated this way, the fuel plan is defensible: real risks, concrete mitigations, and an honest acknowledgment that it is built and proven in the right order rather than assumed.

title: Fuel-Cycle Instrumentation and Monitoring
lede: Sensors along the fuel cycle measure flow, composition, purity, and inventory, turning fuel handling into a measured, accountable process.
body: Every claim made about the fuel cycle — the mix ratio, the purity, the reserve, the mass balance — rests on measurement. Instrumentation is distributed along the loop: flow meters on injection and exhaust, composition analyzers before and after the plasma, purity monitors after separation, and inventory gauges on storage. Together they turn fuel handling from an assumed process into a measured, auditable one.

The measurements serve three systems. Plasma control uses real-time flow and composition to hold the density and mix ratio. Fuel accountancy uses inventory and flow data to keep the helium-3 mass balance closed. Quality assurance uses purity and composition data to gate each batch. Because helium-3 is a scarce, bred, tritium-derived material, this monitoring also supports the material-tracking discipline expected of it — the same sensors that optimize the burn also account for the resource.
Flow, composition, purity, and inventory measured around the loop
Feeds plasma control, fuel accountancy, and quality assurance
Closes the helium-3 mass balance in real time
Supports material tracking of a bred, tritium-derived resource

Instrumentation is the connective tissue of the fuel section: it is what makes every other page's claim — purity, ratio, reserve, balance — a measured fact rather than an assumption, and it is where the fuel supply meets the burner's control brain.
